questions.q: Where does every workflow run for a repository appear in the GitHub UI?
options: The Issues tab
The Actions tab, with the left sidebar listing each workflow by its name: field
Only in the repository's README file
Nowhere -- runs are not visible after they finish
questions.explain: The Actions tab is the central place every workflow run lives, with runs listed newest-first under the workflow they belong to.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say 'someone eventually checks the Actions tab' is not a reliable monitoring strategy on its own?
options: Because the Actions tab doesn't actually show failures
Because GitHub deletes run history after 24 hours
Because only administrators are allowed to view the Actions tab
Because for a pipeline running many times a day across a team, failures on branches nobody's actively watching can sit unnoticed, sometimes for days
questions.explain: Passive 'someone will look eventually' monitoring misses failures on branches that aren't being actively watched -- the lesson's reason for pushing failures to people instead of waiting for them to look.

questions.q: What does the GitHub Actions step condition if: failure() do?
options: It runs the step only if an earlier step in the job failed
It runs the step on every single run regardless of outcome
It deletes the failed job's logs
It retries the failed step automatically up to 3 times
questions.explain: if: failure() scopes a step (like a notification) to only execute when a prior step in the same job failed -- exactly what you want for an alert you don't want firing on success.

questions.q: How do branch protection required checks double as a monitoring mechanism, per this lesson?
options: They don't -- required checks are purely a merge-blocking feature with no visibility benefit
They automatically email the entire company on every commit
A failure becomes visible directly on the pull request itself, blocking the merge button, without anyone needing to separately check the Actions tab
They disable the Actions tab entirely once configured
questions.explain: A required check surfaces its failure right on the PR, serving as both enforcement (blocking merge) and visibility (no separate tab-checking needed) in one configuration.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as a 'flaky test', and why is it worth fixing?
options: A test that passes and fails inconsistently with no underlying code change -- worth fixing before it erodes trust in the whole quality gate
A test that always passes regardless of code changes
A test that only runs once per week
Any test written in a language other than Apex
questions.explain: A flaky test's inconsistent results independent of actual code changes undermine confidence in the gate -- if failures don't mean anything reliable, people start ignoring them, including real ones.
